365.title: Esau runs to meet him (Genesis 33:1–11)
365.hook: Jacob fears revenge, but his brother runs, embraces him, and weeps
365.carry: to see your face is like seeing god
365.howItsDone: Christians often read Jacob and Esau's meeting alongside the parable of the prodigal son, and churches use both when teaching about reconciliation between estranged family members.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night at the river Jabbok, a new name, Israel, and a limp. Your line: wrestle till the blessing.

Morning. Jacob is limping. He looks up, and there it is, the thing he has dreaded for twenty years: Esau, coming with four hundred men. Jacob lines up his family, the servants and their children in front, Leah and hers next, Rachel and little Joseph at the very back, where they'll be safest. Then he walks out ahead of them all, alone, and bows to the ground seven times, each bow a little closer. Everyone has a version of this walk: the call you've avoided, the person you wronged, coming toward you, and you can't read their face.
screen: `FOUR HUNDRED MEN.` → `THE FAMILY IN RANKS.` → `SEVEN BOWS.`

segments.voice: And then Esau runs. In the King James Bible: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." No speech. No list of grievances. The brother who once said he would kill Jacob runs to him. Genesis doesn't explain what changed in Esau, whether he forgave slowly over twenty years or all at once on the road. The silence is part of the gift. Jacob keeps pressing his herds on him. Esau says, "I have enough, my brother; keep that thou hast unto thyself." Jacob insists, and says the line behind today's carry: "I have seen thy face, as though I had seen the face of God, and thou wast pleased with me." Yesterday Jacob named the river Peniel, face of God, because he wrestled there and lived. Now he sees God's face again, in a brother's face he expected to be furious and found full of welcome. Christian readers often hear another story inside this one. When Jesus tells of the prodigal son, the father sees his son far off, runs, falls on his neck, and kisses him: almost the same words. Many hear the father in Esau. And the story stays honest. The brothers don't move in together. They part kindly and live in different places. Reconciliation here is a real embrace, not a perfect ending.

If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

366.title: The coat (Genesis 37:1–11)
366.hook: a favored son, a many-colored coat, and dreams that anger his brothers
366.howItsDone: The Joseph story is often taught to children through the coat, and preachers use Genesis 37 to talk about favoritism and envy in families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peniel: Esau ran to his brother, and your line was to see your face is like seeing God.
screen: `TO SEE YOUR FACE IS LIKE SEEING GOD.`

segments.voice: In some family group chats, everyone knows who the favorite is. The birthday that gets the bigger post. The news that gets three heart emojis from Dad. Nobody says it. Everybody sees it. Jacob's family has a favorite too: Joseph, seventeen, Rachel's first son, born when Jacob was old. Rachel, the wife Jacob loved most, has died. Joseph is out with his brothers and the flocks, and he brings back a bad report about them to their father. Today Joseph's story begins, with a piece of clothing.
screen: `EVERYONE KNOWS THE FAVORITE.` → `JOSEPH, SEVENTEEN.` → `A BAD REPORT.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours." Many colors is the famous version, but translators aren't sure what the Hebrew means. Some modern translations say a long robe with sleeves, the kind you wear when you don't do field work. The same words turn up in Second Samuel, for a robe worn by a king's daughter. Either way, everyone could see it. The coat said, every day, this one is different. And the brothers: "they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him." Then Joseph has dreams. The brothers' sheaves of grain bow down to his sheaf. The sun, the moon and eleven stars bow down to him. And he tells them, both times. Even Jacob rebukes him for the second. But the text adds: the brothers envied him, but his father kept the saying in mind. Nobody in this scene is innocent. A father playing favorites. A teenager who can't keep his dreams to himself. Brothers whose resentment is hardening into something worse. Genesis doesn't make anyone a villain yet. It shows the cost of favor, paid by everyone in the house. Isaac loved Esau; Rebekah loved Jacob. Jacob grew up in a house of favorites, and now he builds another one.

segments.voice: Look at a family, an office, a team or a classroom you're part of: who is the favorite, and who never quite gets the coat? Then the harder part: is there anywhere you're the one handing out coats? See it without judging yourself harshly, think of one small way to even things out, and if you pray, you can ask for a fair heart.
The coat. The special robe Jacob gave Joseph, his favorite son: a sign of love, and a daily reminder to his brothers that they were loved less.

367.title: Into the pit (Genesis 37:12–36)
367.hook: his brothers throw him in a pit and sell him for twenty pieces of silver
367.carry: the pit is not the end
367.howItsDone: Christian tradition has often read Joseph's betrayal as a foreshadowing of Jesus, betrayed for silver, and the story is used in teaching about families torn apart by envy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the coat: a favored son, and brothers who couldn't speak kindly to him. Your line: favor has a cost.

Jacob sends Joseph on an errand: go see if your brothers are all right, and bring me word. They're far from home with the flocks, a long walk north. Joseph gets lost, and a stranger has to point the way. Picture the brothers on a hillside, squinting at a figure in the distance. They know him from a long way off; maybe it's the coat. One of them says, here comes the dreamer. Before he even reaches them, they've decided what to do.
screen: `AN ERRAND FROM HIS FATHER.` → `SEEN FROM FAR OFF.` → `HERE COMES THE DREAMER.`

segments.voice: Their first plan is murder: kill him, throw him in a pit, say a wild animal ate him, and see what becomes of his dreams. Reuben, the oldest, talks them out of it: throw him in alive, he says, secretly planning to come back and rescue him. So they strip off the coat and throw him in. In the King James Bible: "the pit was empty, there was no water in it." A dry cistern. Then the brothers sit down to eat. Joseph is in the hole, and they have lunch. Years later they'll remember hearing him plead. A caravan of traders comes by on its way to Egypt, and Judah asks: what profit is there in killing our brother? Let's sell him. So they sell him for twenty pieces of silver. Genesis names the buyers as Ishmaelites and also as Midianites, and readers still puzzle over how the two fit. Reuben comes back, finds the pit empty, and tears his clothes. The brothers dip the coat in a goat's blood and bring it to Jacob. The man who once wore goat skins to fool his blind father is fooled by a goat. He says an evil beast has devoured Joseph, and refuses to be comforted: I will go down to the grave mourning. And the last line: Joseph is sold in Egypt, to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh. He is alive. The pit was not the end. Some Christian readers hear an early echo of Jesus, betrayed by those close to him for pieces of silver.

368.title: Potiphar's house (Genesis 39)
368.hook: a slave, falsely accused, and yet the Lord was with Joseph
368.howItsDone: Many Christians turn to Genesis 39 in seasons of unfair treatment or unwanted work, and the repeated line "the LORD was with Joseph" is often used in sermons and devotions about God's presence in hard places.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bor: a dry cistern, twenty pieces of silver, and a coat dipped in goat's blood. Your line: the pit is not the end.

Some people end up in work they never chose: a night shift taken because the rent was due, a first job in a city where they know no one, far below what they hoped for. Now make it far worse. Joseph is barely more than a boy, in a foreign country, sold. He's a slave in the house of Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard. Nobody from home knows where he is. His father thinks he's dead. And the chapter's first line about him is not what you'd expect.
screen: `A JOB YOU NEVER CHOSE.` → `SOLD, SEVENTEEN, ALONE.` → `POTIPHAR'S HOUSE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And the LORD was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian." Notice the order. The Lord was with him, and he was still in his master's house. Being with God didn't mean getting out. It meant that where he was, things went well. Potiphar notices, and puts him in charge of everything he owns. Then Potiphar's wife notices him too. Joseph is handsome, the text says, and day after day she presses him to sleep with her. He refuses: his master has trusted him with everything, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" One day, when the house is empty, she grabs his garment. He runs, and leaves it in her hand. His brothers stripped off one garment; now another is left behind, and again clothing is used to tell a lie. She tells the household, then her husband, that Joseph attacked her. Potiphar is furious, and Joseph is thrown into prison. He did the right thing and lost everything again. Then the chapter repeats itself: "But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy." The keeper of the prison puts him in charge of the other prisoners. Twice in one chapter, from the top of a house to the bottom of a prison, the same line. It doesn't promise Joseph safety. It says, twice, that he wasn't alone where he landed.

Picture doing it. If you pray, you can ask God to be with you there; if you don't, notice that you can bring something good into a place you didn't choose.

369.title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
369.hook: Joseph interprets dreams and asks to be remembered, and is forgotten two years
369.howItsDone: Some Christians read Joseph's long wait in prison as a picture of trusting God through delay, and the words "remember me" are part of Christian prayer through the thief's request in Luke 23:42.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Potiphar's house: a slave who did right, a garment used for a lie, and your line, the lord was with him.

A covered shift. A reference letter. A friend talked through a terrible night. And the friend says, I won't forget this. Then weeks go by, and nothing. In Pharaoh's prison, two new prisoners arrive: the king's chief butler, who served his cup, and his chief baker. Both have offended Pharaoh. Joseph, who now looks after the prisoners, is assigned to them. One morning he finds them both miserable, and asks the kind of question a jailer doesn't usually ask: why do you look so sad today?
screen: `I WON'T FORGET THIS.` → `THE BUTLER AND THE BAKER.` → `WHY SO SAD TODAY?`

segments.voice: They've each had a dream, and no one to explain it. Joseph says, in the King James Bible: "Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you." He doesn't claim the gift as his own. The butler dreams of a vine with three branches, grapes ripening, and himself pressing them into Pharaoh's cup. Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you back your job. Then Joseph asks one thing: "But think on me when it shall be well with thee." The Hebrew verb is remember: remember me, mention me to Pharaoh, get me out. I was stolen from my land, he says, and I've done nothing to deserve this pit. Here, for once, Joseph speaks about what was done to him. The baker tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, birds eating from the top one. Joseph doesn't soften it: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head, from off you. On Pharaoh's birthday, it happens exactly so. The butler gets his cup back. The baker is hanged. And the chapter's last line, flat as a closed door: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him." The next chapter begins two full years later. Some Christian readers hear a far-off echo at the cross, where a man dying beside Jesus asks, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. That man is answered the same day. Joseph asked, and waited two years.

370.title: Pharaoh's dreams (Genesis 41:1–40)
370.hook: seven fat cows, seven thin; Joseph plans for famine
370.howItsDone: Christians often point to Joseph's storehouses when teaching about stewardship and wise planning, and many church food banks and savings programs draw on this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph in prison: a butler, a baker, and one request. Your line: remember me.

Two full years go by. Then the most powerful man in Egypt has a bad night. Pharaoh dreams he's standing by the Nile, and seven sleek, fat cows come up out of the river. Then seven thin, ugly ones come up and eat the fat ones, and look just as thin as before. He sleeps again and dreams of seven full ears of grain on one stalk, swallowed by seven thin, scorched ones. In the morning he calls every wise man and magician in Egypt. Nobody can tell him what it means. And the butler, holding the cup, suddenly remembers something.
screen: `SEVEN FAT, SEVEN THIN.` → `NOBODY CAN EXPLAIN IT.` → `THE BUTLER REMEMBERS.`

segments.voice: The butler confesses: I remember my faults this day. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph at once, and Joseph shaves and changes his clothes. The young man who keeps losing his garments gets a new one. Pharaoh says, I hear you can interpret dreams. Joseph answers, in the King James Bible: "It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The same move as in prison: not me, God. The two dreams are one. Seven good years of harvest are coming, then seven years of famine so severe the good years will be forgotten. The dream came twice, he says, because God has settled it. But Joseph doesn't stop at explaining. He gives a plan. Set a wise man over the land. In the seven good years, store up a fifth of the harvest in the cities, kept for the famine. Don't spend all of the good years in the good years. Pharaoh asks his court: "Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?" And he puts Joseph over all Egypt, second only to Pharaoh. This morning a forgotten prisoner; by the afternoon, he runs the country. Christians have read Joseph as a model of faith joined to practical wisdom: he trusts God with the future and still builds the barns. Here, giving God the credit and drawing up a grain plan sit side by side.

371.title: The brothers bow (Genesis 42)
371.hook: his brothers come for grain and don't recognize him; he turns away and weeps
371.howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 42 as a story about guilt surfacing years later, and preachers use the brothers' confession to talk about honesty and repentance within families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pharaoh's dreams: seven fat cows, seven thin, and a prisoner who ended the day running Egypt. Your line: plan for the lean years.

The good years come, and Joseph fills the storehouses. Then the famine arrives, as the dreams said, all the way to Canaan, where old Jacob watches his family go hungry. He hears there's grain in Egypt: why do you just sit looking at one another? Go down and buy some. Ten brothers go. Benjamin, Rachel's other son, stays home. Jacob has already lost one of Rachel's boys; he won't risk the second. So ten men walk into Egypt to stand in line for bread, before the governor of the land.
screen: `THE FAMINE REACHES CANAAN.` → `TEN BROTHERS GO DOWN.` → `BENJAMIN STAYS HOME.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Joseph's brethren came, and bowed down themselves before him with their faces to the earth." The sheaves are bowing, and Joseph remembered the dreams, the text says. "Joseph knew his brethren, but they knew not him." Of course not. He was a teenager in a coat; now he's a grown Egyptian official, shaved, speaking through an interpreter. He speaks roughly, accuses them of being spies, and holds them three days. Then he lets them go, but keeps one brother, Simeon, bound, until they come back with the youngest. And the brothers, not knowing he understands every word, talk among themselves in their own language: "We are verily guilty concerning our brother, in that we saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear." All these years later, the pit is still in the room. Then: "And he turned himself about from them, and wept." The governor steps away so no one sees his face, cries, and comes back to keep testing them. Why test them? Genesis doesn't say. Readers wonder whether he wants to know if they've changed, or is simply hurt and doesn't know what to do yet. Genesis leaves both open. Look at the week behind us: Esau running to his brother, the coat, the pit, Potiphar's house, the forgotten prisoner, the dreams by the Nile. Under all of it sits a family that broke. And now the brothers say out loud what they did.
screen: `THE SHEAVES BOW AT LAST.` · `HE KNEW THEM; THEY KNEW NOT HIM.` · `WE ARE VERILY GUILTY.` · `THE GOVERNOR TURNS AWAY AND WEEPS.` · then, large: `AND HE TURNED HIMSELF ABOUT FROM THEM, AND WEPT.`

segments.voice: Maybe there was a time you turned away so no one would see you cry: at work, at a funeral, in the car before walking into the house. You don't have to cry now; just notice what was being carried then, and how long it was carried alone, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can bring that moment to God; if you don't, be gentle with the person you were then.
Simeon. The brother Joseph holds back in Egypt, kept bound until the others return with their youngest brother.
Your line: he turned away and wept. They saw a governor; he saw his brothers. Until tomorrow.
